population.description: Healthy adults (not specific to resistance training)

gradeRationale.note: Moderate-certainty (GRADE) benefit specifically on MEMORY. No significant effect was found on overall cognitive function or executive function in the same meta-analysis - the statement below is deliberately scoped to memory only, not "brain function" broadly. A 2026 corrigendum/commentary on this same source found the originally-reported attention benefit became non-significant after correcting a statistical double-counting error, which is why attention is not claimed here either.

statement: Creatine supplementation improves memory specifically in healthy adults; it does not show a significant effect on overall cognitive function or executive function in the same evidence base.

citations.title: The effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive function in adults: systematic review and meta-analysis
citations.source: Systematic review and meta-analysis (16 RCTs, 492 participants)

review.note: New evidence domain drafted from master research list v2 (2026-09-05). This required adding a new outcome entity (cognitive_function) since no existing outcome fit memory specifically. Not yet wired into any goal or eligibility policy - there is no current user goal (e.g. a "memory/cognitive support" goal) that this outcome maps to, so this claim currently sits as evidence only and cannot yet surface a recommendation. Whether to add such a goal is a product decision, not made here. The hydration/water-retention angle from the same source review (Ziegenfuss et al., 2003) was deliberately NOT turned into a formal claim - it corrects a misconception (creatine's water retention is intracellular, not subcutaneous bloat) rather than describing a scored, recommendable benefit, so it is better used as explainer copy than as a claim record.
